sources.title: Direct effects of illustrative tax changes bulletin (June 2025)
sources.notes: Methodology notes: direct effects on the tax base and closely related bases; behavioural responses via taxable income elasticities and tax-motivated incorporation; wider economic effects excluded; rate changes scale roughly linearly, allowances and limits do not; CGT and SDLT non-linear and asymmetrical.

sources.title: Compliance review of the Direct effects of illustrative tax changes bulletin (Office for Statistics Regulation)
sources.notes: December 2025 review prompted by concerns about transparency of pre- and post-behavioural estimates; recommends a detailed methodology document and reconsideration of the official statistics label.

sources.title: Schedule of updates and announcements for HMRC's statistics
sources.notes: 6 July 2026 entry: publication of the Direct effects of illustrative tax changes bulletin (due 7 July 2026) deferred to complete a review of the key assumptions underpinning some of the estimates.

sources.title: Statement of Funding Policy: Funding the Scottish Government, Welsh Government and Northern Ireland Executive
sources.notes: Barnett formula (paragraphs 3.9-3.18): change to planned UK Government departmental spending × comparability factor × population proportion, applied to resource and capital DEL separately. Annex B lists the departmental comparability factors used at Spending Review 2025; the FCDO and Ministry of Defence undertake only reserved activities and have none (B.12).

sources.title: Estimated cost of tax reliefs
sources.notes: Table 2 gives six-year cost estimates (£ million, 2020-21 to 2025-26) of each tax relief; the later years are projections. They are estimates of the cost of the relief as it stands, not forecasts of what removing it would raise; see the background quality report.

sources.title: Background quality report: tax relief statistics
sources.notes: Section 4, Accuracy and reliability: "These figures should be interpreted as estimates of the amount of relief which is claimed and subsequently granted each year. These estimates do not represent the gain to the exchequer should a relief be abolished." Costs are on an accruals basis.

sources.title: Autumn Budget 2024 Table 5.1: policy decisions
sources.notes: Certified costings of Autumn Budget 2024 measures, £ million 2024-25 to 2029-30, positive reduces borrowing. Lines used: 24 (energy profits levy package: rate to 38%, investment allowance abolished, sunset to March 2030), 25 (additional-dwellings stamp duty surcharge 3% to 5%), 27 (capital gains tax main rates to 18% and 24% with BADR and IR changes), 29 (agricultural and business property relief reform from April 2026), 30 (inheritance tax thresholds frozen to April 2030).

sources.title: Forecasts for the UK economy: a comparison of independent forecasts
sources.notes: Averages of independent forecasts. Short term: 2026 GDP growth 1.1%, CPI Q4 3.3%, RPI Q4 4.2%, PSNB 2026-27 £119.0bn; 2027 GDP 1.1%, CPI 2.3%. Medium term (calendar years 2026 to 2030): GDP 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, 1.4, 1.5%; CPI 3.1, 2.7, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0%; RPI 3.7, 3.8, 3.2, 2.9, 2.8%; PSNB (2026-27 to 2030-31) £126.4bn, 106.6, 99.5, 90.3, 82.2. HMT states that the averages and ranges may be reproduced free of charge provided they are reproduced accurately and not used in a misleading context; the underlying forecasts remain the copyright of the forecasting organisations.

sources.title: Finance Act 2007, section 1: charge and rates for 2007-08
sources.notes: For 2007-08 the starting rate was 10%, the basic rate 22% and the higher rate 40%.

sources.title: Finance Act 2008, section 1: charge and main rates for 2008-09
sources.notes: For 2008-09 the basic rate is 20% and the higher rate 40%; the basic rate has been 20% since.

sources.title: Finance Act 2012, section 1: charge for 2012-13 and rates for 2012-13 and subsequent tax years
sources.notes: Additional rate 50% for 2012-13 and 45% from 2013-14; basic rate 20%, higher rate 40%.

sources.title: Finance Act 2021, section 5: basic rate limit and personal allowance for future tax years (as amended)
sources.notes: Sets the basic rate limit at £37,700 and the personal allowance at £12,570 for 2022-23 to 2030-31 (the later years added by amendment), switching off indexation for those years.

sources.title: Rates and allowances for Income Tax: current and past
sources.notes: Personal allowance £12,570 and basic rate limit £37,700 in each year 2023-24 to 2026-27; basic rate 20%, higher rate 40% (£37,701 to £125,140 of taxable income), additional rate 45%.

sources.title: Rates and allowances: National Insurance contributions
sources.notes: 2026-27: employee (Class 1) 8% between the primary threshold (£242 a week) and the upper earnings limit (£967), 2% above; employer 15% above the secondary threshold (£96 a week), 13.8% up to 2024-25; Class 4 self-employed 6% between £12,570 and £50,270 and 2% above.

sources.title: Rates and allowances: Corporation Tax
sources.notes: Main rate 25% for profits over £250,000 from April 2023 (19% in 2022); small profits rate 19%; marginal relief between £50,000 and £250,000.

sources.title: Inheritance Tax thresholds and interest rates
sources.notes: Nil-rate band £325,000 from 6 April 2009 to 5 April 2031; £312,000 in 2008-09.

sources.title: Excise Duty hydrocarbon oils rates
sources.notes: Unleaded petrol and diesel 52.95p per litre from 23 March 2022.

sources.title: Capital Gains Tax: rates
sources.notes: Higher and additional rate taxpayers pay 24% on gains from 6 April 2026; basic rate taxpayers pay 18% on gains within their remaining basic rate band and 24% above it.

sources.title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: residential property rates
sources.notes: Single property: 0% to £125,000, 2% to £250,000, 5% to £925,000, 10% to £1.5 million, 12% above; usually 5% on top if you own another residential property.

sources.title: VAT rates
sources.notes: Standard rate 20% since 4 January 2011 (17.5% before); reduced rate 5% (for example children's car seats and home energy); zero rate (for example most food and children's clothes); some things exempt (postage stamps, financial and property transactions).

sources.title: VAT rates on different goods and services
sources.notes: Lists the goods and services at 0%, 5% and 20%: most food and drink, children's clothes and footwear, books and newspapers, passenger transport for 10 or more, construction of new dwellings at 0%; domestic fuel and power at 5%.

sources.title: Alcohol Duty rates
sources.notes: Rates from 1 February 2026 per litre of pure alcohol: beer 1.3% to 3.4% ABV £9.96, 3.5% to 8.4% £22.58, 8.5% to 22% £30.62, above 22% £33.99; still cider 3.5% to 8.4% £10.39.

sources.title: Child Benefit: what you'll get
sources.notes: Weekly rates: £27.05 for the eldest or only child, £17.90 for each additional child.

sources.title: Bank of England Interactive Statistical Database: 10-year nominal par gilt yield (IUDMNZC)
sources.notes: Daily series. 4.63% on 2 January 2026; 5.35% on 11 September 2026; 5.29% on 18 September 2026 (with Bank Rate 3.75%).

sources.title: CPI annual rate, all items (D7G7, MM23)
sources.notes: 2.9% in July 2026 (published 19 August 2026).

sources.title: RPI all items, percentage change over 12 months (CZBH, MM23)
sources.notes: 3.2% in July 2026 (published 19 August 2026).

sources.title: How Inheritance Tax works: thresholds, rules and allowances
sources.notes: The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%, charged on the part of the estate above the threshold.

sources.title: Public Expenditure Statistical Analyses 2025, chapter 4 tables
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. Table 4.3 gives public sector expenditure on services by function in real terms (£ billion, 2024-25 prices) and Table 4.4 the same as a share of GDP, both 2002-03 to 2024-25. Function spending covers the whole public sector, including local government and the devolved administrations, so it is wider than a UK Government department's budget.

sources.title: Benefit expenditure and caseload tables 2026: outturn and forecast tables
sources.notes: Official statistics in development. Table 1a gives expenditure by benefit in nominal terms, 1948-49 to 2030-31, on the same forecast as the OBR’s. The State Pension line is the base for costing a change to how the pension is uprated.

sources.title: International Development (Official Development Assistance Target) Act 2015
sources.notes: Section 1 puts a duty on the Secretary of State to meet the 0.7 per cent of gross national income target for official development assistance. Section 2 covers the accountability to Parliament if the target is not met in a year.

sources.title: Schools, pupils and their characteristics
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. 8,920,227 pupils in all schools, of which 8,355,420 in state-funded schools. 2,214,994 eligible for free school meals on the benefits criteria (26.5% of state-funded pupils). Almost 1.6 million infants took a free meal on census day, of whom over 1.2 million through universal infant free school meals. The state-funded totals are sums of the published school-type rows; the department prints no single state-funded total.

sources.title: Universal infant free school meals: conditions of grant 2026 to 2027
sources.notes: "A meal rate uplift to £2.66 will be implemented for the 2026 to 2027 academic year... An allocation assumes that pupils will take 190 school meals over an academic year, providing £505 per eligible pupil."

sources.title: Free school meals expansion grant: methodology
sources.notes: From the 2026/27 academic year free school meals in England are extended to every child in a household on universal credit, funded with "over £1 billion over the multi-year spending review period from 2026 to 2029". Confirms the schools national funding formula free school meal factor at £505 a pupil a year.

sources.title: Student loan forecasts for England
sources.notes: Official statistics. Table 1 gives loan outlay by product; Table 4b the Resource Accounting and Budgeting charge; Table 4c the transfer proportion, which is the share of loan outlay that scores as government expenditure in the national accounts.

sources.title: Student loans in the public sector finances: a methodological guide
sources.notes: "Splitting lending into two components: a genuine loan and government spending. This new approach recognises that a significant proportion of student loan debt will never be repaid by recording government expenditure related to the cancellation of student loans in the period that loans are issued." The loaned portion is a financial transaction; only the transfer portion scores in borrowing.

sources.title: Changes to tuition fees: 2026 to 2027 academic year and 2027 to 2028 academic year
sources.notes: The maximum tuition fee for a standard full-time course at a provider with a Teaching Excellence Framework award and an access and participation plan is £9,790 in 2026/27 and £10,050 in 2027/28.

sources.title: Nationalising the water sector: how we assessed the cost
sources.notes: "The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) has estimated that nationalising the water industry would cost approximately £100 billion." The regulatory capital value of the sector was £99.3bn in 2024 and £106.7bn in 2025. Defra treats that value as debt plus equity and applies no discount or premium, on the ground that creditors could demand compensation immediately.

sources.title: Monthly statistics on the public sector finances: a methodological guide
sources.notes: Section 5.1.3: "When cash is used to purchase a financial asset of equal value, there is no change to overall indebtedness... Hence there is no expenditure and the transaction has no impact on PSNB. However, there is necessarily a cash payment, which impacts on PSNCR." Section 5.1.4 adds that reclassifying a body into the public sector changes net debt without any cash moving.

sources.title: Consolidated budgeting guidance 2025-26
sources.notes: Chapter 8: financial transactions "do not score as spending and there is no immediate effect on Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities (PSNFL)... This will increase public sector net debt (PSND)". Purchases of equity score in a ringfence within capital DEL. Chapter 3: capital grants score in the capital budget and affect public sector net investment.

sources.title: Spending Review 2025
sources.notes: Confirms £39bn for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme over ten years from 2026-27, reaching £4bn a year in 2029-30; official development assistance falling to 0.3% of gross national income by 2027; and NATO-qualifying defence spending reaching 2.6% of GDP by 2027.

sources.title: Social and Affordable Homes Programme 2026 to 2036: policy statement
sources.notes: "could deliver around 300,000 affordable homes over its lifetime, with around 180,000 for Social Rent." At least 60% of homes must be for social rent. The department does not publish standard grant rates: "we are not publishing standard grant rates".

sources.title: Affordable housing supply in England: 2024 to 2025
sources.notes: National Statistics. 64,762 affordable homes completed in England in 2024-25, the highest since 2014-15, of which 12,198 for social rent, the highest since 2012-13.

sources.title: A wealth tax for the UK: Wealth Tax Commission final report
sources.notes: Advani, Chamberlain and Summers. Table ES.2 and Table 8: an annual wealth tax above £10m at 1.12% raises £9.9bn with low avoidance and £8.7bn with high avoidance, from 22,000 taxpayers, before administration costs. Section 6.3 warns that its analysis "has been constrained by a lack of reliable data on individuals with total wealth above £10 million".

sources.title: Revenue and distributional modelling for a wealth tax (Evidence Paper 13)
sources.notes: Advani, Hughson and Tarrant. Table 1 gives the annual wealth tax rates and revenues. Section 3.1: behavioural responses to a 1% rate are assumed to cut the tax base by 7% to 17%, the low and high avoidance scenarios. A 10% non-compliance rate is applied separately.

sources.title: Household total wealth in Great Britain: April 2020 to March 2022
sources.notes: The wealthiest 1% of households hold at least £3,121,500, which is the highest threshold published; nothing is published about wealth above £10m. "Estimating aggregate household wealth can be difficult as the wealthiest households can be underrepresented." Accreditation of the survey was suspended from this round in June 2025.

sources.title: Inheritance Tax liabilities statistics
sources.edition: Estates passing on death in 2023 to 2024
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. Table 12.1a: 220 taxpaying estates above £10m in 2023-24 paid £1,040m of inheritance tax, 15% of the total, at an average effective rate of 18%, lower than the 25% paid by estates between £3m and £7.5m.

sources.title: Universal Credit quarterly statistics, 29 April 2013 to 14 May 2026
sources.notes: 8.4 million people on Universal Credit in May 2026. By immigration status, 84.5% are in the Common Travel Area group (UK, Ireland or right of abode); with the EU Settlement Scheme and indefinite leave to remain the three account for 96.2%, "in line with the general principle that only people who are settled in the UK or protected by the EU Exit Withdrawal Agreement should be able to claim Universal Credit".

sources.title: Public funds
sources.notes: "The NRPF condition means you will not be able to claim most benefits, tax credits or housing assistance that are paid by the state." Contributory benefits, including the state pension, are not public funds and can be claimed by people with no recourse to public funds who have the contribution record.

sources.title: UK to deliver on 5% NATO pledge as Government drives greater security for working people
sources.notes: "With the new 5% commitment on national security, the UK expects a projected split of 3.5% (core defence) and 1.5% (resilience and security) to be agreed at the NATO summit, with a target date of 2035."

sources.title: Statistics on International Development: provisional UK official development assistance spend 2025
sources.notes: Accredited official statistics. UK aid was £13,036m in 2025, 0.43% of gross national income, down from 0.50% in 2024. The UK spent 0.7% of national income on aid from 2013 to 2020. 18.3% of aid in 2025 was spent inside the UK on refugee and asylum costs.

sources.title: Independent Water Commission: final report
sources.notes: The Cunliffe review. Water companies will spend £104bn on investment and operation over the five years to 2030, about £44bn of it enhancement. Footnote 569 gives the sector capital value as £103bn in 2024-25. Paragraph 684 records that the review was barred by its terms of reference from considering public ownership.

sources.title: Financial Stability Report
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Quoted: moves in gilt yields were "amplified by hedge fund deleveraging" during the most volatile period after the onset of the Middle East conflict; global sovereign issuance at historically high levels with higher proportions at shorter maturities; "any negative change in expectations could have wider consequences for sovereign debt markets". Bank of England material; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Bank Insights: What were the drivers of UK long-term interest rates in 2025?
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Quoted: "the primary driver of the increases in long rates was higher term premia"; rises "can largely be attributed to global factors, such as geopolitical uncertainty and concerns around fiscal sustainability"; 30-year yields at their highest since the turn of the century. Bank of England material; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: The policy landscape 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Quoted: "As John Healey puts together his first Budget, the backdrop of bond market turmoil limits the room for manoeuvre"; "£1 in every £12 of public spending now goes on debt interest"; "With energy bills rising again this winter, the cost-of-living crisis is back centre stage". Resolution Foundation; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Chancellor letter to the Treasury Select Committee: Budget 2026 date
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. The Chancellor commissioned the OBR to "prepare an economic and fiscal forecast for publication on 28 October 2026. This will be accompanied by the Budget." Also: "Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security. That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East."

sources.title: Change: Labour Party manifesto 2024, Strong foundations
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. The tax lock verbatim: "Labour will not increase taxes on working people, which is why we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT." Also the two fiscal rules and the path to 2.5% of GDP on defence. Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Change: Labour Party manifesto 2024, Kickstart economic growth
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "Labour will cap corporation tax at the current level of 25 per cent, the lowest in the G7, for the entire parliament." "1.5 million new homes over the next parliament." National Wealth Fund £7.3bn. Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Change: Labour Party manifesto 2024, Build an NHS fit for the future
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "40,000 more appointments every week"; "patients should expect to wait no longer than 18 weeks from referral for consultant-led treatment"; a "National Care Service, underpinned by national standards". Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Change: Labour Party manifesto 2024, Break down barriers to opportunity
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "Recruit 6,500 new expert teachers in key subjects"; "3,000 new primary school-based nurseries"; free breakfast clubs in every primary school; a child poverty strategy. Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Andy Burnham's first speech as Prime Minister
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "Put life's essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again." "We will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down." "issue my first instruction: to end rough sleeping in our country." "a more preventative state". "Later this year, I will bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan".

sources.title: PM statement to the House of Commons, 1 September 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "We cut VAT on electricity bills and cut business rates for pubs, social clubs, and live music venues." "the defence of our nation will always be my first priority." "Our bedrock of our approach will be grounded in fiscal responsibility." Sentencing: "anyone convicted of manslaughter, death by dangerous driving or indecent assault will not see change to their prison term."

sources.title: Prime Minister's speech on social care, 29 July 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "A national care service... that sits alongside the National Health Service". "The government has agreed a fair pay agreement for social care staff to come in financial year 2028-29". "Around 2 million adults have unmet care needs". The Casey review brought forward to summer 2027. No new funding figures announced.

sources.title: New PM cuts tax on household electricity bills to give breathing space on cost of living
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. VAT on domestic electricity cut from 5% to 0% from 1 October 2026; about £45 a year off a price-cap bill; costs about £850 million in 2026-27; funded by cancelling the Digital ID programme (£1.8bn over three years); reduces CPI by about 0.10 percentage points.

sources.title: Build Back Better: Our Plan for Health and Social Care
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-20. The 2021 plan for a levy: "a UK-wide 1.25 per cent Health and Social Care Levy based on National Insurance contributions"; "Together with the increase to the rates of dividend tax, the Levy will make available around an additional £12 billion per year on average for health and social care across the UK". The levy was legislated in 2021 and repealed before it took effect as a separate tax; the £12 billion is HM Treasury's own figure for it, averaged over 2022-23 to 2024-25 and inclusive of the dividend rise.

sources.title: £2 bus fares from January 2027
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "single bus tickets will be capped at £2 in England outside London from 1 January until 31 December 2027"; "The new £2 cap is backed by £400 million of extra government funding"; "funded by savings from reprioritising the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero's budget, including by switching funding for international climate from grants to loans".

sources.title: Free bus travel 24/7 for disabled people as Prime Minister takes further action to ease cost of living
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Time restrictions on disabled bus passes in England removed from 1 April 2027; £60 million (£40m DWP, £20m DfT).

sources.title: The Defence Investment Plan: funding explainer
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "the UK will spend 2.7% of GDP on core NATO defence spending"; "the UK has committed to reach 3.5% of GDP on defence spending by 2035"; 3% in the next Parliament; "It is funded primarily by reallocating budget from across government departments, with £10.3 billion identified now. A further £4.7 billion over four years will be confirmed at Budget 2026, in a fair and balanced way." Total MoD budget £297.7bn over four years.

sources.title: Budget 2025 speech
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "I will not be increasing National Insurance, the basic, higher or additional rates of Income Tax or VAT"; "We are lifting 450,000 children out of poverty with the end of the two-child limit"; "I will more than double the headroom against our stability rule to £21.7 billion"; "I know that maintaining these thresholds is a decision that will affect working people."

sources.title: Budget 2025
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Two-child limit removed from April 2026, lifting 450,000 children out of poverty, rising to around 550,000 with other measures; stability rule met in 2029-30 by £21.7 billion and the investment rule by £24.4 billion; thresholds frozen for a further three years from April 2028 to April 2031.

sources.title: Support for children and young people with special educational needs
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "DfE estimates that some 43% of local authorities will have deficits exceeding or close to their reserves in March 2026"; "a cumulative deficit of between £4.3 billion and £4.9 billion when accounting arrangements that stop these deficits impacting local authority reserves are due to end"; high-needs funding up 58% in real terms between 2014-15 and 2024-25 to £10.7 billion; "the current system is not achieving value for money and is unsustainable". NAO material reproduced under its terms with attribution.

sources.title: Education, health and care plans: reporting year 2026
sources.notes: Published June 2026 (exact day not recorded). Fetched 2026-09-16. 718,838 children and young people with active EHC plans at 15 January 2026, 12.5% higher than at January 2025, the highest annual percentage increase since EHC plans were introduced in 2014.

sources.title: An analysis of the asylum system
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "the current direct cost of supporting people seeking asylum is disproportionately high (£4.0 billion in 2024-25)". NAO material reproduced under its terms with attribution.

sources.title: Personal Independence Payment: official statistics to April 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "4 million claimants entitled to PIP (caseload) in England and Wales" at 30 April 2026, a 2% increase on 31 January 2026; psychiatric disorders 39% of claims; entitlement "has increased steadily since the introduction of PIP in April 2013".

sources.title: Timms review of Personal Independence Payment: interim report, Annex B, DWP evidence pack
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "in FYE 2026, estimated DWP expenditure on working age people receiving these benefits was £25 billion – mostly PIP, covering 3.2 million people"; "PIP has been difficult to forecast since its introduction"; "even with quite large reductions in new awards to PIP, there would still be considerable growth in caseload and spending over the next few years".

sources.title: John Healey, tax and Budget 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. Notes "Labour's manifesto commitments not to raise rates of income tax, national insurance or VAT"; that the previous Chancellor "left a wafer-thin amount of headroom against her fiscal rules which evaporated post-budget"; and that "The OBR's forecasts that will accompany the budget are likely to have deteriorated since March". Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Chancellor John Healey's growth speech, 7 September 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "The Prime Minister and I are in lockstep in our commitment to meeting the fiscal rules at the upcoming Budget." "at the Budget I will set out a roadmap to fiscal devolution". "There's nothing progressive about the government spending £1 in every £10 on debt interest." "Since 2022, we have been paying that trust penalty". The speech does not mention headroom or the manifesto.

sources.title: Budget to move power and money out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain." "It will be built on fiscal discipline." "It will meet our fiscal rules."

sources.title: PM sets out plan to end waiting list backlogs through millions more appointments
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. The Elective Reform Plan baseline: a waiting list of 7.5 million; 65% of patients treated within 18 weeks by the end of the following year as the interim target; 9 in 10 within 18 weeks by the end of the Parliament; 2 million extra appointments in the first year (40,000 a week).

sources.title: Northern Powerhouse Rail to drive biggest travel upgrade in the North in a generation
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. £1.1 billion over the Spending Review period for planning, development and design; a £45 billion programme funding cap; £120 billion of capital investment for infrastructure this Parliament; benefits from the 2030s.

sources.title: Over £69 billion confirmed for council budgets
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. "Over £69 billion in funding for England's councils has been confirmed" for 2025-26; a 6.8% cash-terms increase in Core Spending Power; up to £3.7 billion additional funding to social care authorities including an £880 million uplift to the Social Care Grant.

sources.title: Burnham drives defence to deliver security and growth in every postcode with £8.4bn nuclear submarine investment
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-16. £8.4bn nuclear submarine investment; 22,000 apprenticeships by 2035. "Keeping this country safe is the first responsibility of any government".

sources.title: Vehicle tax rate tables
sources.notes: Cars registered on or after 1 April 2017: standard annual rate £200 (single 12 month payment) after the first year; expensive car supplement an extra £440 a year for five years. Published by DVLA on GOV.UK.

sources.title: Rates and allowances for Air Passenger Duty
sources.notes: Page updated 1 April 2026. Reduced (economy) rates from 1 April 2026: domestic £8, band A £15, band B £102, band C £106; from 1 April 2027: £8.26, £15.49, £105.33, £109.46.

sources.title: Excise Duty: tobacco duty rates
sources.notes: From 6pm on 26 November 2025: cigarettes £353.50 per 1,000 plus 16.5% of retail price, minimum excise duty £471.93 per 1,000 (about 57p more on a packet of 20).

sources.notes: Standard rate 12%; higher rate 20% on travel insurance, certain insurance sold with mechanical or electrical appliances and certain motor vehicle-related insurance.

sources.title: Private pension statistics: Table 6, estimated cost of pension income tax and National Insurance contribution relief
sources.notes: £ million by tax year, 2019-20 to 2024-25. Gross income tax relief on contributions and fund investment income, National Insurance relief on employer contributions split by class (employer £14,300m and employee £4,800m in 2024-25, plus £3,400m and £1,000m on salary-sacrificed contributions), the tax charged on pensions in payment, and the net figure. Static costs of the reliefs as they stand, not the yield from removing them.

sources.title: Call of duties
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-19. On capital gains tax: "when assets are held until death, any built-up gains are written off for tax purposes. This creates perverse incentives to avoid realising gains, and is a particularly valuable tax concession to those with very large business wealth. Instead, full tax should be paid whenever beneficiaries later realise gains." And, of ending the death write-off together with a settling-up charge on emigrants: "The combination of these two measures would raise an estimated £4 billion a year". The Foundation publishes no split between the two. Resolution Foundation; quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: PAYE and corporate tax receipts from the banking sector: 2025
sources.notes: Table 1, £ billion by financial year. Bank Levy receipts: 2016-17 3.0, 2017-18 2.8, 2018-19 2.6, 2019-20 2.5, 2020-21 2.3, 2021-22 1.5, 2022-23 1.3, 2023-24 1.4, 2024-25 1.3. Bank Surcharge receipts: 2016-17 1.1, 2017-18 1.8, 2018-19 1.9, 2019-20 2.0, 2020-21 1.4, 2021-22 2.3, 2022-23 2.6, 2023-24 1.4, 2024-25 1.0. The commentary: "Bank Surcharge receipts were £1.0 billion in financial year 2024 to 2025, a decrease of £0.5 billion (32.6%) on the previous year, which mostly reflects the full effects of the reduction in the Bank Surcharge rate from 8% to 3% in April 2023 and lower UK banking sector profits". A 2026 edition was not published at 19 September 2026; check the landing page on or after 25 September 2026.

sources.title: Corporation Tax Act 2010, section 269DE: surcharge allowance
sources.notes: The bank surcharge allowance is £100,000,000 for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2023, substituted for £25,000,000 by Finance Act 2022 section 6; the surcharge is charged on a banking company's profits above the allowance.

sources.title: VAT on fuel and power (VAT Notice 701/19)
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. "On 21 July 2026, the government announced a temporary zero rate of VAT for Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales) for domestic supplies of electricity and other supplies of qualifying use. The temporary zero rate applies from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027." Northern Ireland stays at 5%.

sources.title: Temporary zero rate of VAT for domestic electricity in Great Britain
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. "This measure introduces a temporary zero rate of VAT for qualifying supplies of domestic electricity in Great Britain, for the period 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027. The rate will remain 5% on all other types of domestic fuel UK-wide." Revenue and Customs Brief 10 (2026) accompanies it.

sources.title: Equalising National Insurance on partnership income: revenue and distributional effects
sources.edition: Advani, Gazmuri-Barker, Lonsdale and Summers, 4 September 2025
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. Centre for the Analysis of Taxation. "Levying ‘Partnership NICs’ would raise an estimated £1.9 billion in 2026-27, after accounting for behavioural responses and interactions with other taxes"; static yield £2.4bn at a zero elasticity, £1.9bn at 0.25; "Almost half the revenue raised from introducing Partnership NICs would be raised from partners in the top 0.1%"; "Only impact one third (34%) of current partners"; the design is an equivalent of employer NICs on partnership profits with a Partnership Allowance equal to the £10,500 Employment Allowance. Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Reforming Capital Gains Tax: Revenue and Distributional Effects
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. Centre for the Analysis of Taxation. The package: equalise CGT rates with income tax, a rate-of-return investment allowance, remove the uplift at death, charge CGT on emigration, abolish BADR and Investors’ Relief, reform losses. "We estimate that if our policy package is implemented in full it would raise an additional £14bn per year in total revenues across CGT and Income Tax. This is our central estimate"; "best thought of as a medium-term effect using the 2025/26 static tax base"; Table 5, rate of return allowance: dynamic tax revenue £30.6bn, additional revenue £14.3bn (88%); "Under our worst-case scenario (largest behavioural response) we estimate an additional £9.7bn"; "These estimates do not account for CGT from trusts and non-resident individuals." Written before the 30 October 2024 rise of the main rates to 18% and 24%. Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Business Owners who Emigrate: Evidence from Companies House records
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. Centre for the Analysis of Taxation. "The UK is an international outlier in not charging Capital Gains Tax (CGT) on people who leave the country. Just among UK nationals, the business shareholdings of leavers are worth more than £5 billion. This is costing the UK at least £500 million per year in foregone CGT, although the true figure is likely to be much higher"; "in the year we studied, almost three-quarters came from just 10 people". Quoted briefly with attribution.

sources.title: Public sector finances, UK: August 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. "Borrowing ... was £18.3 billion in August 2026; this was £2.9 billion (19.0%) more than in August 2025 and £3.5 billion above the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecast. Borrowing was £77.3 billion in the financial year (FY) to August 2026; this was £2.2 billion (2.7%) less than in the same period last year but £8.1 billion above the OBR forecast." Public sector net debt provisionally £2,985.5 billion at the end of August 2026.

sources.title: New Chancellor faces £10 billion headroom headache as public sector finances remain on a knife-edge
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-22. The Foundation’s estimate that the energy shock had cut the March headroom of £23.6 billion to about £10 billion. Resolution Foundation; quoted briefly with attribution, for context only.

sources.title: Labour mansion tax raid to hit homes worth £1.5m (City AM)
sources.notes: Press coverage used only as qualitative context. Reports The Times: government sources called lowering the surcharge threshold to £1.5 million a "live discussion" in the Treasury; the number of homes caught "would reach 271,000 based on current values", "nearly 300,000 homes" in the headline figure.

sources.title: Budget 2026: which taxes will Burnham and Healey hike? (City AM)
sources.notes: Press coverage used only as qualitative context. Names the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation as the source of the £14bn for aligning capital gains tax with income tax; lists "vape shops crackdown, online sales levy and warehouse business rates tax" as measures the July business-rates announcement deferred to the Budget; reports the pension tax-free lump sum and a bank surcharge rise as under discussion.

sources.title: Death and taxes: the Autumn Budget and reform of inheritance tax (Evelyn Partners)
sources.notes: Professional-firm commentary used only as qualitative context. "One option the government has been widely reported to be considering is a 10% “death tax” that would replace the inheritance tax regime", with the National Care Service "estimated to require additional spending of £18.5 billion annually and rising"; the government has said it has no plans. No costing of the levy is published.

sources.title: What if Andy Burnham lowered the mansion tax threshold to £1.5m?
sources.edition: Tax Policy Associates analysis, 7 July 2026, updated 19 September 2026
sources.notes: Fetched 2026-09-23. "Our estimate: a £1.5m threshold would tax around 160,000 additional homes on an OBR-scaled basis, almost doubling the number of properties in scope." Static revenue in 2028-29: £605m for the announced £2m tax, £850m with a £1.5m band at £1,500 and other bands unchanged, £1,270m with a £1.5m band at £2,500 and every other band pushed up (TPA’s base case); after the OBR’s retention ratio (£400m ÷ £605m) and £40m a year of valuation and administration costs the base case "could roughly double the net revenue, to about £800m". "This is our illustrative extrapolation, not an OBR forecast for a £1.5m tax." Quoted briefly with attribution.
